content:
RAG vs. CAG, clearly explained!

RAG is great, but it has a major problem:

every query hits the vector DB. even for static information that hasn't changed in months.

this is expensive, slow, and unnecessary.

Cache-Augmented Generation (CAG) fixes this by letting the model keep static information in its key-value (KV) memory, which is what the model builds internally for every token it reads.

in fact, you can combine RAG and CAG for the best of both worlds.

here's how it works:

RAG + CAG splits your knowledge into two layers.

↳ static data (policies, documentation) gets cached once in the model's KV memory

↳ dynamic data (recent updates, live documents) gets fetched via retrieval

you get faster inference, lower costs, and less repeated work.

the trick is being selective about what you cache.

only cache static, high-value knowledge that rarely changes. cache everything and you'll hit context limits. separating "cold" (cacheable) and "hot" (retrievable) data keeps this system reliable.

you can start today. OpenAI and Anthropic already support prompt caching in their APIs.

one thing to know before you scale it.

prompt caching matches on an exact prefix, byte for byte. your cached layer only gets reused when it sits at the very front of the context in the same order every time.

↳ reorder two cached policy documents and both turn into a miss

↳ cache document A alone and document B alone, then query both, and the second one misses because the model computed its cached state without ever seeing the first

in production this looks like a small fraction of your cached blocks serving almost all the hits. the rest just sits there.

the way out comes from how attention behaves. tokens attend mostly to their own local neighborhood, and only a few reach across document boundaries. CacheBlend recomputes those few and reuses everything else from the separately cached documents.

multi-document queries run two to four times faster, quality holds, and order stops mattering.

it ships in LMCache, which is fully open source.

repo: https://t.co/TXlaLLu04a

(don't forget to star 🌟)

below, i have quoted my article on KV cache management. it covers where prefix caching stops working and how a proper caching layer fixes it.

give it a read.

content:
AI doesn't start with the LLM.
It starts with the Data engineering underneath it.

Here are 7 ways Data Engineering powers modern AI applications:

1. Data Ingestion

AI applications need data from databases, APIs, SaaS tools, logs, and event streams. Tools like Kafka, Airbyte, Fivetran, Debezium, Kinesis, and Pub/Sub move that data into systems where it can actually be used.

2. Data Processing & Transformation

Raw data is rarely AI-ready. Python, SQL, Spark, PySpark, Databricks, dbt, Snowflake, BigQuery, and Delta Lake help clean, join, transform, and structure massive datasets.

3. Embeddings & Vector Search

For semantic search and RAG, documents are transformed into embeddings and stored in vector databases such as pgvector, Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Qdrant, or Elasticsearch. This allows AI systems to retrieve information based on meaning, not just keywords.

4. RAG & LLM Applications

A production RAG system needs much more than an LLM. Data engineers build pipelines for document parsing, chunking, metadata extraction, embedding, indexing, retrieval, reranking, and freshness using tools like LangChain, LlamaIndex, LangGraph, OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, and Grok.

5. AI Coding Assistants

Tools like ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Codex, and Gemini CLI need structured access to repositories, documentation, dependencies, code history, and project context. Data pipelines help turn massive amounts of information into usable context.

6. Training & Fine-Tuning Data

Better models require better datasets. Data engineering handles cleaning, deduplication, validation, tokenization, dataset versioning, synthetic data generation, and feature pipelines before the data reaches the training process.

7. Data Infrastructure & Observability

AI systems operate on constantly changing data. Airflow, Dagster, Kubernetes, Docker, AWS, Azure, GCP, MLflow, OpenTelemetry, and data-quality tools help orchestrate pipelines, monitor failures, track lineage, and keep AI systems reliable.

The LLM gets the attention.
The data engineering layer makes the AI useful, scalable, and reliable.

AI without good data engineering is just a powerful model sitting on top of messy data.

title: For anybody curious as to why I do not use AI tools in my work, it's not for lack of trying. I have been getting a lot of questions regarding why I don't use LLMs in my work, because to most people, t
content:
For anybody curious as to why I do not use AI tools in my work, it's not for lack of trying. I have been getting a lot of questions regarding why I don't use LLMs in my work, because to most people, theoretically my work should be fully replaceable by LLMs, right?

Even though I personally find the societal implications of AI to be very unsavory, I have tried to approach AI models for specific purposes. I have been working behind the scenes to test out various AI models which might serve as a way to get indications and warnings for world events I might have missed, or to synthesize large blocks of text. For the record, I am ardently anti-AI for actual content generation; I will NEVER use an LLM to write my work for me. More generally, I approached LLMs as a tool, and I wanted to keep an open mind to not turn down any force-multiplier that might be useful.

Unfortunately, this has been a nightmare.

It's just not worth exploring for the topics that I have to cover. So far, I have spent countless hours framing prompts, providing direct sources myself, and coaching both Claude and ChatGPT along, tailoring prompts for hours....all for neither to actually provide one single useful indicator that I did not know about already. If you don't want me, and instead want a clanker to summarize the threat environment, go for it, but you won't get the truth in the vast majority of cases. To me, all of the AI models are time-wasters for this task...If I need to spend 20 minutes framing a prompt so that the LLM will take it and actually do what I want, I could spend 20 minutes working on my own, and get vastly more work done. LLMs have uses, but for this stuff, it's a hard no.

These LLMs are simply lobotomized to the point that they are unusable for my line of work.

And honestly, I think the whole AI game has become rather sad. I frequently have people DM me, and they are using an LLM to speak to me. As in, they will take my texts, paste them into an LLM, and have it generate the response. Literally, for each message (and we're talking short messages too).

To me, that's the most heartbreaking thing that I see on a nearly daily basis. I have to deliberately tell people to just talk to me, and to not feed my texts into LLMs. Some people want the machine to consume them, they want to be replaced by a faceless machine, they want the "blue" pill...and AI is letting them have it. To me that's devastating and one of the main reasons why I do not support the trajectory that LLMs are on. They could have been good tools, and certainly still can be in very specific and controlled circumstances. But the mainstream models that are used by most people are not actually helping civilization, and in fact are almost certainly going to be our downfall.

AI is already re-writing history in real time, and now it's eroding the fabric of humanity itself.

content:
BREAKING: Claude opened a new position in Vista Energy at Wednesday's open, $70.50, sized at 7.6 percent. It is now the largest stock position in the book after Vistra.

Why Claude bought it:

"Vista is the biggest independent oil producer in Vaca Muerta, the Argentine shale field. Output is compounding about 17% a year, from 158 thousand barrels a day this year to a guided 208 by 2028, at a lifting cost of $4.50 a barrel and a 70% cash margin. Nearly three quarters of the oil is exported at international prices. You pay about 3.6 times this year's expected cash earnings and 7 times next year's profit for that. American shale producers growing at low single digits trade at 4.5 to 6 times.

That discount is the price of Argentina. Argentine government debt yields roughly 4.7 to 5.1 percentage points above US Treasuries, a two-month high, and the peso still runs inside a managed band. My case is that the gap narrows in steps as three things get proven out: the production ramp gets delivered (the second quarter already came in at 156 thousand barrels a day against a 158 full-year guide), the new export line turns landlocked barrels into shipped ones with a first cargo scheduled for January 2027, and the IMF program holds through the September review.

The part I like most is the floor. Assume investors never pay a cent more per dollar of earnings than they do today. Growth and debt paydown alone get the stock to about $76 in a year. Everything above that is the Argentina discount closing, and I am not paying for it up front.

My probability-weighted target is $85, which sits 14% below the $98.78 average analyst target. This works without the Street's number.

What would make me wrong: Brent oil sitting at $65 to $75 for most of the next year while Argentina cracks again, the IMF review slips, and spreads blow past 6 percentage points heading into the 2027 election. That combination puts the stock near $50, down 28%. I carry that branch at 29%, and that is why the position is 7.6% rather than the 10 its ranking would allow.

One honest note: the stock ran 8.8% in the five sessions before I bought, mostly on a large investor turning up in quarterly filings rather than anything about the business. It gave back 3% in Wednesday's session. I am starting slightly underwater, and I bought it for the twelve months, not the week.

content:
How to prompt Claude Fable-5 (and any AI model):

→ Start by deleting the long examples you give.
→ Delete the "step-by-step" prompt technique. 
→ Avoid biased questions. Don't finish with "right?"
→ Chain-of-Thought (step-by-step) only works well with maths problems. It's worth skipping it.
→ Don't give a long list of rules (max 3) to follow. 

The models got very good at simple prompts, and worse at your complicated, over-structured ones.

To make a simple prompt, better:

→ Make your next prompt shorter.
→ Define the goals with extreme clarity.
→ Give no more than 3 rules to perform one task.
→ Ask open-ended questions to let it figure it out.
→ Always encourage it to ask clarifying questions.
→ Don't trust the sources blindly. It tries to prove itself by finding links that agree with what it already has written.

This is the one simple prompt template I stick to:

"[GOAL: What a finished answer must achieve. Write the test it has to pass.]
[CONTEXT: The facts the AI would otherwise invent. Only the ones it cannot know.]
[CONSTRAINTS: The hard limits. 3 max.]
If anything here is missing or unclear, ask me before you answer.
[Add “use AskUserQuestion tool” if you’re on Claude]."

I've been teaching prompt engineering since 2022, and so much has changed since then.

What was true - because science said so - isn't anymore. The models are 10x more capable now.

I'm a psycho so I actually filter out and read the 100+ daily papers on prompt engineering (on arxiv. org). Read my findings at https://t.co/BhdLRaCgvy.

once these agents begin performing economic work, they will also need the ability to receive money, hold assets, make payments, trade and allocate capital

today’s financial system was never designed for autonomous systems like these

it depends on bank accounts, borders, business hours, manual approvals and human identity

this is where blockchains change the equation. blockchains turn money and markets into internet-native infrastructure that is global, programmable and always on

this is why i am fully convinced that the agent economy will naturally run on crypto rails

but that is only the beginning

the important thing to understand is that these agents will operate continuously, 24/7. they will transact more frequently than humans and generate economic activity at machine speed and internet scale

and those txns must be fast and inexpensive enough to make even the smallest actions viable

most financial infrastructure, including most blockchains, was not designed for this level of autonomous activity

sui can process independent transactions in parallel and scale horizontally with demand. it allows agents to combine multiple actions into a single atomic txn

sui gives agents a composable financial environment where they can move between assets, markets and applications

but agentic finance will also create an entirely new class of security problems. the way sui was designed gives us a major advantage in solving them

i will give you a much clearer idea of what this means at sui basecamp next month

the larger point is that we are not building sui simply to bring today’s financial system onchain

we believe AI will create billions of autonomous economic actors and that they will need a financial system built specifically for how they operate

we are building sui to be that system

content:
A guy used ChatGPT for 2 years before a coworker told him to try Claude.

He signed up. Free account. Typed a question. Got an answer. Thought: "Same thing, different logo."

He used Claude for 6 months like that  typing questions, reading answers, closing the tab. Every conversation started from zero. Every chat disappeared the moment he moved on. He never opened a single setting. Never explored a single feature beyond the text box.

His coworker  a product designer who'd been using Claude daily for over a year  watched him work one afternoon and said:

"You're using a $20/month thinking partner like a search engine from 2010. You've never set up a Project. You've never used an Artifact. You've never turned on Memory. You've never tried Deep Research. You've never customized how Claude talks to you. You haven't built a single workflow. You're typing the same context into every conversation because you don't know the platform remembers who you are now."

She said the gap between a casual Claude user and someone who actually understands the platform is the difference between asking a stranger for directions every morning and having a colleague who already knows your entire job.

"Claude isn't a chatbot. It's a workspace  with memory, persistent projects, interactive documents, web research, file creation, custom styles, and an entire agent system that can work on your files while you do something else. Most people never get past the text box. The text box is about 10% of what this thing actually does."

Here are the 13 features she showed him that changed how he uses Claude entirely: 🧵👇

Underrated life hack: literally just do things.

Not "consume more content about doing things." Not "wait until you feel ready." Just actually do the thing.

Most people spend 10x more time researching how to start than they do actually starting.

Want to learn AI? Stop watching another video. Open Claude and try to automate one task you did today.

Want to start a business? It's as simple as selling something to a stranger.

Action generates information that consumption never can.

You learn ten times faster doing a bad first attempt than reading a hundred perfect examples.

The gap between people who "know a lot about" something and people who actually do it is almost never talent.

Just do the thing. Fix it as you go.

content:
Chamath was given a simple choice, 100 shares of Anthropic, 100 shares of OpenAI, 100 shares of SpaceX, pick one stack (Save this).

He picked SpaceX without hesitation, and his reasoning is worth unpacking fully because it cuts to the heart of how the best investors think about technology bets.

His take on OpenAI and Anthropic was actually generous.

He acknowledged that Anthropic is the superior enterprise product, his own fund uses it as their foundational model and that ChatGPT has built one of the most powerful consumer brands in the history of technology.

But the case for SpaceX is built on something completely different, it is not one business, but rather a platform for multiple businesses that compound off each other.

Starlink generated $11.4 billion in revenue in 2025, growing roughly 50% year over year, and represented 61% of SpaceX's total $18.7 billion in revenue.

The EBITDA margin on the connectivity segment hit 63%, compared to 38–39% for the largest traditional telecom companies on earth.

Subscriber count went from 2.3 million in 2023 to over 10.3 million by Q1 2026, spanning more than 160 countries, and revenue is projected to reach $15.5 billion in 2026.

@chamath core insight is that the global communications infrastructure is profoundly broken and he is right.

Roughly 2.6 billion people globally still lack reliable internet access, and even in developed markets, rural connectivity is patchy, expensive, and controlled by legacy monopolies with no incentive to upgrade.

Starlink is a replacement cycle for an entire layer of global infrastructure that has barely changed in 30 years.

Every maritime vessel, every commercial aircraft, every military unit, every rural hospital, every developing-world government that wants connectivity now has one viable option that didn't exist five years ago.

The maritime and aviation segments alone carry ARPUs of $250 to $25,000 per month per customer, orders of magnitude above the consumer subscription.

But Chamath's most interesting point is what he called embedded optionality, the idea that SpaceX's business model doesn't stop at earth.

SpaceX now has the only fully reusable heavy lift rocket system in the world with Starship, and it is the only company currently capable of launching the next generation of Starlink V3 satellites that carry roughly 10 times more capacity than the current constellation.

Every new market SpaceX opens on earth, direct to cell with T-Mobile, enterprise contracts, government agreements becomes a template that can theoretically be replicated the moment humans establish a permanent presence elsewhere.

A Starlink equivalent for a lunar base, a Mars colony, or an orbital station is  the same product with a different launch address.

Anthropic and OpenAI are betting on winning a model race where the finish line keeps moving while SpaceX is betting on owning the physical infrastructure layer of the next era of human civilization, on earth and eventually beyond it.

One of those bets has a floor and the other doesn't and that is why Chamath picked @elonmusk's SpaceX.

content:
WTF, GROK BOT JUST MADE AI AGENTS AVAILABLE TO LITERALLY ANYONE – CREATING CONTENT HAS NEVER BEEN THIS EASY, EVEN IF YOU'VE NEVER MADE ANYTHING BEFORE

Content was never a talent problem. It's a headcount problem.

One person doing research, design, copy, analytics, timing and publishing – that's six jobs. The switching between them is what kills consistency, not a lack of ideas.

Here's what one of these setups actually looks like.

A Chief of Staff sits in the middle and routes every task. Nothing lands on the human.

→ Researcher tracks what's actually moving and pulls real sources instead of guesswork
→ Writer turns that research into finished copy, ready to review
→ Visualiser gets fed a few reference visuals once, then ships everything in that style
→ Analyst reads the numbers and tells the rest of the team what worked
→ Scheduler owns timing and holds the queue
→ Publisher ships it

The part that makes it work: every agent on Grok Bot gets its own persistent computer, browser and file system – and they all share memory.

So the research is already sitting inside the draft before the draft starts. No copy-pasting between tools. No approving every step. No human in the middle.

You can even teach an agent a repetitive task by recording yourself doing it once. Start recording, do the thing, stop. It learns the pattern.

And that's the real shift.

Nobody needs AI to tell them what to post.

They need it to delete the 40 steps between the idea and the post.

Everyone has a backlog of things they've meant to make for months. This is what starts clearing it.

content:
Joe Rogan uploads 2 to 3 hour episodes. You see 30 second clips. Someone cut them.

Creators pay $29 a month for AI to do that job.

A solo developer in China gave it away for free.

The repo is called AutoClip. 6,391 stars on GitHub. 1,253 forks. MIT licensed.

Every clip you save from a podcast, stream, or interview was cut from something longer. Streamers do not go viral from streams. They go viral from clips of streams. A 2 hour episode holds 15 to 25 viral clips. Finding them by hand takes 4 to 6 hours.

Here is what AutoClip does.

Paste a YouTube link. Or a Bilibili link. Or drop in a local video file. The AI reads the whole transcript, scores every moment for viral potential, cuts the highlights, adds captions, and hands you a folder of vertical shorts ready for TikTok, Reels, and YouTube Shorts.

Here is what makes it different from OpusClip.

- Runs locally on your laptop. Your footage never leaves your machine.
- Works with OpenAI, Google Gemini, Alibaba Qwen, or SiliconFlow. Pick whichever LLM is cheapest for you.
- No credit system. No monthly minutes cap. Process a 4 hour livestream if you want.
- MIT licensed. Fork it. Ship it in a product. Sell it. No permission needed.
- Docker one-line install. Runs in a browser tab at localhost:3000.

The stack: FastAPI backend, React frontend, Celery task queue, Redis, SQLite, yt-dlp for downloads, FFmpeg for cutting. One developer named zhouxiaoka wrote 89 commits and shipped the whole thing.

Here is the interesting part.

OpusClip raised $68 million in venture funding from SoftBank, Samsung Next, and DCM Ventures to build a subscription business around this exact workflow. The whole short form video AI market is priced like a SaaS product because most creators do not know an open source alternative exists.

One person in Hangzhou wrote it in his spare time and put it on GitHub. Six thousand people have starred it. One thousand two hundred have forked it.

One honest note. Last commit was 77 days ago on June 3. The maintainer is one person. Some features on the roadmap are still marked in development. If you want a polished product with a support team, pay OpusClip. If you want to own the tool that clips your videos, download this tonight.

The people who own the software own the workflow.

Your videos. Your AI. Your shorts.

One Architecture Diagram That Explains Every AI Agent
 
After building and scaling real agent systems in production, the same architecture keeps showing up — no matter the model, framework, or use cas
content:
One Architecture Diagram That Explains Every AI Agent
 
After building and scaling real agent systems in production, the same architecture keeps showing up — no matter the model, framework, or use case.
 
So I mapped it out.
 
This is the universal anatomy of almost every AI agent:
 
→ Perception Layer — how the agent receives input (text, APIs, sensors, events) 
→ Reasoning Engine — the LLM that thinks, plans, and decides 
→ Planning Module — breaks goals into actionable steps 
→ Tool Execution / Action Layer — where the agent actually does work (APIs, code, databases, files, external services) 
→ Memory System — short-term context + long-term knowledge 
→ Guardrails & Safety — permissions, rate limits, human-in-the-loop, content filtering 
→ Observability Layer — traces, logs, metrics, cost & latency monitoring
 
Most people still focus only on the RAG. In production, the real complexity (and risk) lives in how these layers interact and constrain each other.
 
This pattern applies to: 
• OpenAI / Claude 
• Coding agents 
• Custom enterprise agents 
• Multi-agent systems 
• Fully autonomous workflows
 
If you’re building or scaling agents, this mental model will save you a lot of pain.
 
Save this. You’ll need it.

content:
Our entire 20-person GTM engineering org runs on: 

• Claude Code
• Agents
• MCPs 
• Skills

None of this is as complicated as the words make it sound.

Here are the 11 most important terms that’ll put you ahead of the curve.

• CLAUDE(.)md: a text file of instructions Claude reads at the start of every session
• Hooks: rules that fire automatically, like blocking a campaign launch without approval
• MCPs: live connections between Claude and your tools, like HubSpot, Slack and Instantly(.)ai
• Skills: instruction files for repeatable tasks, so SOPs but for Claude
• Scheduled tasks: recurring tasks in the Claude app that run locally
• Routines: the Claude Code version of scheduled tasks, and these can run in the cloud
• Sub-agents: workers Claude delegates to, each with its own context window
• Agent teams: multiple Claude sessions running in parallel, sharing a task list and messaging each other
• Plugins: your setup bundled in GitHub, so the team gets it automatically
• Managed agents: Claude-hosted agents loaded with your full company context and tools
• Agents SDK: Claude Code as a library, for building your own products on top

Your entire media library, searchable by memory instead of filename, running right on your own machine.

It’s a local-first AI file agent called MUZIM. Instead of managing folders, you work with what's actually inside your photos, videos, and documents.

Here's how it comes together in a real workflow:

You get back from a two-week trip with 2,000 photos and clips on your camera. You point MUZIM at the folder, and it builds Collections on its own, by place, by people, by day. Nothing gets moved from where it already lives.

A week later you want "the sunset shot where everyone's laughing." You don't remember the filename. So you just describe it.

Vibe Search understands what's inside your media and takes you straight to that moment, even the exact second inside a video. Once the local model is downloaded, this part runs fully offline, connected or not.

Then you turn it into something. Connect your own Claude or GPT key, and the online AI Agent pulls the best shots from that trip and drafts a highlight video, an X thread, or a recap. Through MCP, compatible tools work with authorized context without re-uploading gigabytes of raw video - saving massive input tokens while keeping raw files strictly local.

The whole idea:

search and organization run locally, on your device the AI workflows run when you want them, on your own key your raw files never leave your machine

Cold storage becomes a private workspace you actually control.

It's called grok-plugin. Basically it's an MCP server that logs in through xAI's OAuth device f
content:
Someone built a way to hand work from Claude Code straight to Grok, and you never touch an xAI API key.

It's called grok-plugin. Basically it's an MCP server that logs in through xAI's OAuth device flow, so it runs on the SuperGrok or X Premium login you're already paying for. And the login happens inside the chat. The link just shows up the first time Claude tries to delegate something, so you approve it and you're done.

So what you get is two tools and one agent.

grok_delegate hands Grok a question, some research, or code to write
grok_review takes your diff or a file and gives you an outside read on it
And the grok-reviewer agent goes further, since it checks Grok's findings against your actual code first and only reports back the ones that actually hold up

There's also a proxy mode that flips the whole thing around. So you run grok-bridge serve, then the grok-claude launcher, and now Claude Code itself is running on Grok. Plain claude stays on Anthropic, so nothing global changes on your machine.

But read the caveats first. The upstream it talks to isn't a documented public API, so it can break whenever xAI changes something. And Grok can't see your workspace, it's text in and text out.

It's 8 days old with 36 stars, which is either early or a warning, I honestly can't tell yet.

3 forks, 1 open issue, MIT License.

content:
This graph is mostly correct but also very misleading. The two extremes don't read the AI-generated code for totally different reasons.

The one on the left doesn't read the code because they can't. They just prompt the AI with "Build X" and "Fix this" and "add that." They couldn't investigate the code even if they wanted. They can't ship scalable and reliable software.

The one on the right doesn't read the code because they know how to steer the AI agents correctly. They provide specific instructions on architecture and implementation, design tests, etc. Occasionally, they look at code, but mostly they know how to get the results they want from the agents.

The one in the middle hasn't yet adapted to the AI wave. They are still working in the past paradigm, using AI as an autocomplete instead of a coding assistant.

content:
Sam Altman made the case for open-source harnesses in July.

a month later, someone shipped it, and it's more efficient than most managed harnesses.

here is the problem it was aimed at:

a large share of your agent's token bill is the model rereading things it already read.

that isn't the model's doing. the runtime around it decides what goes into every prompt and how often the model gets called.

for example, an agent queries a CRM at step four and gets back 400 rows. those rows get piled up in the conversation history.

by step nineteen, the model has to read those rows fifteen times unnecessarily, and every token read is billed at input rates.

it happened because your harness assembled that prompt on every turn and kept the rows in it.

that gives you two levers: how much context the harness carries forward, and how often it calls the model.

there are four practical ways to keep the prompt from growing unnecessarily:

→ load tool schemas on demand. a server with 100 tools doesn't need to put all 100 into every prompt when the agent only calls two.

→ offload large results to disk. turn a large response into a short preview and a file path instead of replaying the entire result on every turn.

→ delegate to subagents. let a subagent spend thirty tool calls in its own context and return one summary to the root agent.

→ run toolchains in code. one script calls three tools, joins the results, and returns a table instead of three turns each dragging a full response.

but reducing context is only half the job. you also need to control how often the model gets called.

a good harness should avoid unnecessary planning, verification, and reflection when the work can be completed in fewer steps.

@TrueFoundry's open-source agent harness, TrueForge, is built around both of those controls.

it sits between the model and the tools, deciding what goes into every prompt and when another model call is actually needed. it also breaks token usage down across the harness, skills, instructions, tools, and messages.

DevRev's Enterprise-Bench is where this gets tested, on multi-step tasks of the kind where an agent pulls records from one system and reconciles them against another.

TrueFoundry ran TrueForge there against Claude Managed Agents, both on the same model, and both finished the same number of tasks.

the tie is the part that matters, because it means the gap underneath is not a quality tradeoff.

TrueForge reached that score on close to a third of the tokens, with roughly 40% fewer trips back to the model. for the same result, that comes out around 2.7x cheaper than Claude Managed Agents.

swapping in an open model made it sharper still. TrueForge with GLM-5.2 scored a little higher than either setup above, and the entire benchmark run cost about $3 at list prices.

being open source matters beyond the license here. the model underneath can be swapped without rewriting the agent, and the whole thing can run inside your own environment when the data cannot leave it.

all of this comes down to the runtime around the model, the context it carries, the tools it exposes, and how many times it goes back to the model.

that is what a production harness actually owns.

the full task list, the per-run numbers, and the MIT-licensed code are on GitHub: https://t.co/Ueo1InZH7M

(don't forget to star 🌟)

you can read more about the same in the article quoted below.

thanks to the TrueForge team for working with me on this one.

1️⃣ I don’t remember where or when, but Mike Green (@profplum99) observed that the impressive, fast and steep adoption of LLMs since 2022 is highly
content:
Here’s the problem with both Anthropic and OpenAI:

1️⃣ I don’t remember where or when, but Mike Green (@profplum99) observed that the impressive, fast and steep adoption of LLMs since 2022 is highly misleading: most of the usage, say 99%, consists of people asking questions they would otherwise ask Google. One can expect this share of the pie ultimately to be claimed back by Google.

2️⃣ Meanwhile, those who use ChatGPT or Claude for more than simply asking questions, say for drafting assistance, brainstorming on complex topics, coding, etc., are growing frustrated with the declining quality. Those are the 1% top users.

3️⃣ The reason quality is going down is most likely that both companies have to throttle inference because they are losing money on each request and facing an increasingly adverse fundraising environment. That’s true even for paid plans.

4️⃣ In other words, those who really need LLMs for the value they can add, the 1%, are having their usage constrained so that OpenAI and Anthropic can absorb the load of the 99% who pay nothing. It’s a loss on both counts: no money is made from the 99% (good luck catching up with Google on advertising revenue), while the 1% are growing disgruntled because of slop, itself the result of inference throttling.

5️⃣ The problem both companies face is very familiar to anyone versed in business strategy or marketing: bad segmentation, which in turn leads to bad strategic positioning.

6️⃣ That’s where the situation diverges. Anthropic can still decide to become 'The AI-Assisted Coding Company' and turn into some combination of Stack Overflow, GitHub and AWS. (They could even acquire GitHub from Microsoft.) I’m not sure they’ll find the TAM necessary to deliver ROIC to their shareholders, though, if the only market they serve is coding.

7️⃣ Meanwhile, OpenAI is in a bind. I don’t see how they catch up with Google in a two-sided, advertising-revenue business aimed at consumers, and I don’t see how they’ll manage to segment their offering and reach a point where there is sufficient willingness to pay across all segments. This is why there are now talks of OpenAI going down, and in any case, I'd say it is all but certain they’ll never generate an ROIC. Cc @edzitron 

8️⃣ Last year, I wrote a long piece explaining how OpenAI could reposition itself to specialize in trading for compute: a Glencore for the AI age. That’s a very large TAM, but I’m not seeing anything that suggests they’re going in that direction. See: https://t.co/eE9z80NvdE

9️⃣ All of the above has been made clear by what @sameer_singh17 calls the "open model summer" 👇 Between Alex Karp’s remarks on CNBC, the emergence of cheap and readily available open-source models, and the gradual shift towards running local models, a battle that will likely be won by Apple, what had until now been discussed by only a few people (Sameer, @ganeumann, and yours truly) has now become obvious to everyone. I wrote about Karp's remarks here: https://t.co/BJlz1qQKgN

🔟 How do you call a bubble out of which the winners are two pre-existing “synergy companies”, Google and Apple (to borrow Jerry's exact words, in reference to @CarlotaPrzPerez's "synergy phase" of a great surge of development) and perhaps only a scaled-back Anthropic refocused on code? A late-cycle bubble. That’s what AI is.

So stop talking about a new technological revolution and see AI for what it is: an incredible, value-adding final iteration of the age of semiconductors, computing and networks, which won’t live up to the hype from an frontier lab ROIC perspective but will still deliver tremendous productivity gains over the next two decades.

We built it with one developer in six months.

content:
A PE firm asked us to rebuild an enterprise kitchen management platform for a company that powers chains like KFC.

We built it with one developer in six months.

Their Product Owner had vibe-coded the first version of the platform in Replit without any engineering background, and it worked well enough to win a pilot with a QSR chain running hundreds of locations.

Then the QSR chain needed it production-grade, certified, and deployed across hundreds of restaurants at enterprise scale. A vibe-coded Replit prototype wasn't going to get there.

We put one AI Velocity Pod on it: one developer and one PM.

Week one, we mapped the entire codebase before writing a line. 

The PO had built working features, but the architecture underneath couldn't support what their contract demanded: multi-location deployment, role-based access across restaurant brands, and real-time demand forecasting.

We rebuilt the foundation and kept every working feature intact. 

The PO kept building in Replit alongside our developer, which meant two parallel code streams feeding into one quality gate. Every line, whether agent-generated or from the PO's Replit sessions, got reviewed against production standards before it shipped.

In six months, one developer delivered:
1. Real-time demand forecasting and inventory management across hundreds of restaurant locations
2. Automated food safety labeling and compliance workflows
3. Cross-restaurant analytics and operational task management
4. Full multi-location deployment with role-based access, ready for enterprise QSR rollout

AI compute: $200 per developer per month.

A company that's been building kitchen technology for 20 years had one of our developers build their next platform. 

The PE firm behind them has now sent us four portfolio companies, each one referred by the last CTO.

That's what the Velocity Framework was built for.

content:
AI SAFETY EXPERT REFUSED TO NAME THE YEAR HUMANITY LOSES CONTROL, AND HIS REASON IS BETTER THAN ANY DATE

roman yampolskiy, ai safety researcher, got pushed to bet on a year. he didnt bite:
"you want something to have a clickable title. scientist says 2027, you will die. that will get you views"

and thats the whole game right there. he's not saying ai is safe, he takes the risk dead serious, hes saying the exact date is the part nobody can actually know, too many things can speed it up or slow it down

the way i see it, the internet doesnt reward the most accurate take, it rewards the most confident one. "nobody knows exactly when" is a weak headline, "AI KILLS YOUR JOB IN 2027" prints. so the most made up part of any prediction, the date, is exactly the part that goes viral

and notice its always the interviewer digging for the number. agi in 2027, jobs gone by 2030, extinction by whenever. not because the number means anything, but because doubt doesnt sell and a clean date does

funny part is the clip itself probably has some scary year slapped on the title. the thing he's mocking is the thing carrying his words across the timeline

A world where Microsoft, Amazon, and Google are the only ones building compute is a world where Nvidia is slowly being squeezed by a handful of customers all simultaneously developing custom chips to replace Nvidia GPUs entirely.

Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium and Microsoft's Maia all exist for one reason, to cut Nvidia out of the stack and Jensen knows it so he is playing a long game most investors haven't registered yet.

Nebius is that fish because it's the only neocloud operating at hyperscaler scale while remaining fully purpose-engineered for AI workloads from silicon to software.

When Google approached neoclouds about deploying TPUs, Nebius said no, its Chief Revenue Officer noting that demand is 99% for Nvidia GPUs and that TPU interest comes almost entirely from former Google employees rather than the actual market.

That alignment with Nvidia's ecosystem, at this scale, with this backlog, and this level of strategic backing  is why Nebius sits in a category of one among the neocloud field.

Patel framed the broader play correctly, every neocloud that survives makes Google's TPU and Amazon's Trainium structurally weaker simply by existing and five years from now, the winners will have reshaped the entire compute landscape in Nvidia's favor.

content:
Compute is the new microscope.

@nebiusai and similar AI clouds are already accelerating drug discovery, gene editing, mental health care, and cancer research in ways that were impossible a few years ago.

AI isn’t just chatbots and image generators, and we have GPU clusters powering the next wave of medicine.

a few examples:

- @swordhealth  is using Nebius AI Cloud and @nebiustf  to run Dawn, a large scale AI mental health agent, and Thrive for musculoskeletal recovery.
Real patients, real clinical AI, running on dedicated AI infra.

- @PrimaMente trained Pleiades, the first foundation model on DNA methylation (epigenetics), on 256 NVIDIA H200 GPUs at Nebius.
their goal is to help with earlier detection of diseases like Alzheimer’s and precision therapeutics that actually understand the chemical language of the genome.
neuroscience at AI scale.

- @CompugenInc (immuno-oncology) trained models on Nebius to predict spatial immune features in tumors.
it helps them uncover previously invisible patterns that help identify new drug targets for patients who don’t respond to existing cancer therapies. from code to clinic, faster.

- Helical is building “Virtual AI Labs” on Nebius.
Their Helix mRNA foundation model (trained in days/weeks instead of months) turns months of wet lab work into hours of virtual experiments. Pharma and biotech teams can now personalize biology foundation models to their own data at unprecedented speed.

Nebius also integrates NVIDIA BioNeMo, offers HIPAA-compliant environments, and runs the AI Discovery Awards, giving GPU credits to startups in biopharma, genomics, medical imaging, and digital health.

This is not theoretical, this production infra is in the hands of researchers and clinicians already. 

The pattern is clear:

1. Traditional clouds weren’t built for the continuous, high-bandwidth, GPU-dense workloads of modern biology.

2. Purpose-built AI data centers + full-stack software are removing the bottleneck.

3. Faster models → faster experiments → faster therapies.

AI and data centers aren’t “coming to healthcare.”
They’re already powering it, from mental health agents and epigenetic foundation models to molecular generation and automated gene editing.

The companies that master this infrastructure will help decide how quickly the next generation of medicines reaches patients.

title: (personal take alert) A weird thing is happening in a lot of AI data center discourse where a meaningful chunk of the industry has taken a lot of the initial criticism pretty seriously and you're seei
content:
(personal take alert) A weird thing is happening in a lot of AI data center discourse where a meaningful chunk of the industry has taken a lot of the initial criticism pretty seriously and you're seeing  changes in water use tech, grid impact, community investment etc but overall the reaction has been pretty 'f*ck you anyway'. 

It reminds me a bit of my early corporate days working for Meta when everyone was saying the company had no interest in safe policies/products and so Meta responded by putting a ton more resources into safety, to which zero critics of the company cared at all and there was zero vibe/tone/policy shift. Downstream of that I think a prevailing sentiment within the company was that a lot of the criticism itself was in bad faith and that this ultimately stalled momentum for a lot of worthwhile safety efforts. 

I don't have a point other than that when overall vibes and sentiment bear no real relationship to real world policy changes or (especially) outcomes, it's easy to wind up with a lot of misaligned incentives and a pretty awful discourse all around. Data center builders/investors should continue to improve the way  those investments are made to make sure they're beneficial to the communities, states, and the country they're being built in simply because that's the right thing to do, regardless of whether those changes are met with accolades or scorn. 

But I also think it's genuinely important for folks to have the capacity to think it's good if there's responsiveness to criticism since that's (hopefully) the underlying point of criticizing stuff. My overall worry is that criticism (not just in AI but across a bunch of spaces) is increasingly existing independently of an interest in incremental improvement and that seems not great.

A 21-year-old computer science student in Helsinki bought his first PC in early 1991 and immediately hated the operating system it came with. So he sat down to write his own.

On September 25, 1991 he posted a quiet message to a Usenet newsgroup announcing what he called "just a hobby, won't be big and professional like GNU."

35 years later that hobby runs every Android phone on Earth, every supercomputer on the TOP500 list, the entire backend of the internet, the International Space Station, and SpaceX's Falcon rockets.

His name is Linus Torvalds. The hobby is called Linux.

Here is the story, because the man who runs the most consequential codebase in human history almost no longer needs an introduction inside engineering and still walks the streets unrecognized everywhere else.

Linus was born in Helsinki, Finland on December 28, 1969. He was named after Linus Pauling, the only person in history to win two unshared Nobel Prizes, in Chemistry and in Peace. He joked he might also be partly named after Linus van Pelt from the Peanuts cartoon. His family was unusual. Both parents were journalists. His grandfather was a statistician. Another grandfather was a poet. The family belonged to Finland's Swedish-speaking minority. There are fewer than 30 people in the world with the surname Torvalds, and according to Linus, they are all related.

At 10 he started programming on his grandfather's Commodore VIC-20. By his teenage years he was writing his own assemblers, editors, and games. He served in the Finnish Army for his mandatory national service and rose to the rank of Second Lieutenant. Then he enrolled at the University of Helsinki to study computer science.

In early 1991 he bought a personal computer with MS-DOS and disliked it intensely. He wanted UNIX, the operating system he had used at the university. UNIX cost thousands of dollars. He could not afford it. So he started writing his own.

He posted the now-famous announcement to comp.os.minix in August 1991. He called the kernel Linux, a portmanteau of his name and MINIX. He released the source code under the GPL license. Anyone could download it, read it, modify it, and ship it for free.

Within a year hundreds of developers around the world were sending him patches. Within five years Linux was running web servers. Within ten years it had taken over the supercomputer market. Within twenty years it was running on most of the internet. Today every Android phone on Earth runs the Linux kernel. Every Chromebook runs Linux. Most of AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure runs Linux. Every Tesla runs Linux. Every SpaceX Falcon 9 and Dragon capsule runs Linux. The International Space Station runs Linux. Every supercomputer in the world's TOP500 list runs Linux.

That was the first thing he built.

In 2005 the proprietary version control system the Linux community had been using, BitKeeper, revoked its free license. Linus was furious. He sat down and wrote a replacement in 10 days. He called it Git. The first commit was on April 7, 2005. Today Git powers GitHub, GitLab, and the source control of every major software organization on Earth. Every line of code at OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, and Microsoft flows through Git. Every AI model on the planet is versioned with software a Finnish engineer wrote in less than two weeks.

He won the 2012 Millennium Technology Prize, the equivalent of a Nobel Prize for engineering. He won the IEEE Computer Pioneer Award in 2014. He completed his master's degree from Helsinki along the way, with a thesis titled "Linux: A Portable Operating System." He moved to the United States, became a citizen, and now works from his home in Portland, Oregon, employed by the Linux Foundation.

A Finnish student announced a hobby project on a message board in 1991.

His code is now in every pocket on the planet.

He still writes most of his important communication on the Linux kernel mailing list.

title:
AI is about to make one part of science incredibly cheap:

Being wrong.

Today, generating a good scientific hypothesis takes time, expertise and money.

AI changes that.

Soon we may be able to gener
content:
AI is about to make one part of science incredibly cheap:

Being wrong.

Today, generating a good scientific hypothesis takes time, expertise and money.

AI changes that.

Soon we may be able to generate 10,000 plausible molecules, proteins or biological hypotheses before breakfast.

Great.

Now which ones actually work?
That requires experiments.

Scientists.
Labs.
Assays.
Greenhouses.
Field trials.
Animal studies.
Clinical trials.
And ultimately, reality.

AI can generate another hypothesis in seconds.

Biology doesn’t suddenly run 1,000× faster because ChatGPT does.

Which means something interesting happens as AI gets better:

Hypotheses become abundant. Evidence becomes scarce.

And the bottleneck in science moves.

From generating possibilities…to experimentally eliminating them.

The most valuable scientific infrastructure of the AI era may therefore not be another foundation model.

It may be the infrastructure capable of answering the one question AI cannot answer by prediction alone:

Is it actually true?
Welcome to the evidence economy.

title:
The Proof of Reality event at AGI Bar brought people together for a simple but important conversation around AI agents and the information they rely on.

The focus was on what happens when agents move
content:
The Proof of Reality event at AGI Bar brought people together for a simple but important conversation around AI agents and the information they rely on.

The focus was on what happens when agents move beyond demos and start doing real work.

One thing that stood out was the need for agents to know whether the information they receive can actually be trusted.

Because an agent can only be as useful as the data it works with.

If the information is incomplete, outdated, or difficult to verify, even a capable agent can make poor decisions.

That makes verification an important part of building reliable AI systems, not just an extra feature.

The event also touched on how users can keep control over information they have already verified instead of having to prove the same thing again and again.

This matters because verified information can become more useful when it can be reused without forcing users through the same process every time.

There was a good mix of people in the room, listening, asking questions and sharing their own thoughts.

It was also a chance to see these ideas explained in a much more practical way, rather than just talking about AI in theory.

@verona_dev was part of that conversation, alongside the other teams involved in the event.

Events like this are useful because they bring the ideas out of the screen and into conversations with real people.

Beijing definitely had a good Sunday, and this felt like one of those discussions that will keep going long after the event ends.

title:
Been seeing a wave of many projects quietly laying off their team across crypto lately

Quite a few are friends and wanted to offer some thoughts for anyone affected or trying to break in the space

1
content:
Been seeing a wave of many projects quietly laying off their team across crypto lately

Quite a few are friends and wanted to offer some thoughts for anyone affected or trying to break in the space

1. Important things to recognise
• Crypto today is very different compared to 2-4 years ago. Gone are the days when you can try to larp as a APAC lead without institutional connections or a DeFi lead raking in $200k a year doing (basically) nothing
• AI + mature tooling = a team of 10 now can do what 30 did in 2021. Most jobs that are cut are mostly being automated or absorbed and are not coming back. Keep that in mind when planning for future careers
• The north star for every company is revenue. Most crypto companies are vapourware (dead L1/L2, another prediction market/perp dex wrapper or some larp AI project) and are unable to fundraise from VCs these days and without cashflow your days are numbered
• You are now competing with TradFi talent, not crypto anons anymore. With banks, asset managers, and payments companies entering and using crypto, the "institutional BD" and partnerships seats are being filled by ex-Goldman/ex-Stripe people. On-chain finance will only survive through integrations with institutions and traditional finance

2. Scenario 1: if you are breaking into the space as a fresh grad or coming from another industry
• Start writing. Structuring your thoughts and putting them into long form writing shows initiative and thought leadership + clear thinking. Have had tons of friends (and also me personally) hired off Twitter (X) just by providing value in public. While it may not directly get you a job, it could open other doors for you to ultimately land a role. That's the reason why I started this account + @mementoresearch with @bobthedegen_ which has been one of the best decisions in our life
• Do targetted work. Pick 3-5 protocols you genuinely understand (perps/ prediction markets/ AI) and write a memo - growth plan, APAC expansion breakdown, a competitive comparison (specific to their situation), and send it to the founder directly. Even rejections can turn into warm network that could be useful!
• Send proof of work. Instead of “Hi, are you hiring?”, send: “I spent some time looking at your APAC growth. Here are 12 potential partners, the 4 I would prioritise, who the decision makers are and how I would approach them"
• Offer a paid trial if you cannot get the full-time role. A 4 week sprint for example for both parties to evaluate team/culture fit
• Train your professionalism. Crypto has a bad rep for the lack of professionalism or unqualified “anons” who may not have worked in a “proper” company. Simple stuff like making a professional CV, understanding how interviews are conducted and preparing well for them and even learning workplace etiquette is essential for landing a role in this time and age
• Learn to sell. Even going for interviews is selling yourself to potential companies. Being able to bring customers, capital, and users is an extremely defensible moat
• The best crypto entry job might be at a bank. The highest-leverage entry point could be the digital-assets desk at a bank, asset manager, or payments company. You get structured training, a reputable and lindy brand name for your CV which will be helpful if you exit into crypto-native roles later. Other than banks or trad companies, another path could be to find early stage AI/robotics companies
• Learn the institutional language. Stablecoin payments, tokenised funds, custody - all boring subjects but in the way crypto is heading towards, you need to brush up your knowledge on these sectors
• Refine your edge. Perhaps you have unique insights in Asia/ able to bring LPs and TVL from HNWIs from this region that will be helpful for a DeFi project. Or you relocated to an untapped region (LATAM, Africa) and are able to offer projects a way to expand into these markets (case in point: how @0xbenito_ is doing work for @BNBCHAIN in the LATAM region - his initiative to learn Spanish + network in LATAM is helpful for a more “Asian” based ecosystem; or @0xCheeezzyyyy with his easy to digest infographics make him a very sought-after content creator)
• Agency. If you are not born into a rich family, there is basically no safety net unless you take steps to save yourself. Are you willing to go on the ground to conferences/local events and network to find a job? Are you willing to put in the 10,000 hours to learn all you can about crypto/AI? Is there a gap in the market that you identify and can exploit?
• Endure the suck. Its a bear market now and companies are saving costs to extend their runway. An alternative is to take whatever job that lands at your desk first (to extend your own runway), but continue to search for better opportunities while working
• Learn AI. Funny to type this, but have seen so many friends not integrating AI into their workflows (heck some of them don’t even pay for AI, it’s a flex these days to have an AI subscription I realise). You gain so much knowledge by vibe coding/ building dashboards -> I even have a friend that monetises this skill by vibe coding for mom and pop companies, just depends on how badly you want it
• Be the XXX guy. Who's known for Dune dashboards - @Adam_Tehc or AI analysis - @0xSammy. Pick a niche and make sure you are good covering it as it makes you legible as a hire (even smaller content creators like @matrixthesun got traction for covering DeFi protocols that eventually got him a job at a perp dex) 

3. Scenario 2: if you were recently laid off / fired
• Preserve your career evidence. Write the numbers behind projects you worked on while they're fresh: “generated XXX qualified leads,” “closed xxx TVL,” “grew X from A to B by xxx strategies,” etc
• Negotiate a good comp package first before signing anything. Unvested tokens, cliff acceleration, severance payment for your runway, NDA/non-compete scope. Also make sure to get a good reference letter from your previous boss
• Audit your runway. Count your months/ emergency savings, cut burn immediately, and plan out your job search strategy. Knowing your number is what buys you the ability to be selective of the next role you take and not to panic
• Create a personal CRM excel sheet. Previous bosses, colleagues, investors, portfolio founders, clients. Categorise these people into order of priority to reach out to
• Lean into your network. If you were at a fund, ask some of your portfolio companies if they have available roles. Or if you were at a project, reconnect with companies you partnered with for roles. Network outside the crypto bubble too (fintech, payments, AI)
• Announce to your friends about your layoff. Ask them to be on the lookout or send your CV to companies that are hiring. Don’t worry about the shame, retrenchment is common in any industry!
• Post on Social media (X or LinkedIn). “My role was affected by the restructuring at X. Worked on A/B/C and achieved the following results. I'm now looking for X roles and particularly interested in Y"
• Contractual work. Any odd jobs/ side hustle that you can do to earn some extra bucks while searching for your next role?

4. Misc
• The games in crypto are solved and token market cap ceilings are getting lower and lower. The chances of making it from memes/on-chain altcoins is rarer as these days p much only bundles/insiders benefit and relying on this alone may not cut it anymore (this is peak bear market talk from me, wen bottom)
• Controversial (and only if you have buffer savings) but is it time to start your own company? Being on the operator side provides unique insights as to how businesses are run. Did you perhaps learn something that you can build yourself together with your ex colleagues or identified a gap while you were at your role?

Truly trying times with this bear market + AI accelerating the number of layoffs. Most people quit here because they are unable to make it through the first hard moment that comes up. This discomfort that you are in won’t last forever, I promise you that.

P.S. I am hiring a full stack and mobile dev for a gamified commerce platform that I am building, if you are interested please send your CV and profile to my DMs (please no PDFs for opsec reasons)

title:
AI in drug development is moving beyond isolated use cases and becoming a portfolio of decision support capabilities across the full development lifecycle.

In discovery, AI supports target identifica
content:
AI in drug development is moving beyond isolated use cases and becoming a portfolio of decision support capabilities across the full development lifecycle.

In discovery, AI supports target identification, molecule design, screening, and lead optimization.

In nonclinical development, AI supports toxicity assessment, pharmacology modeling, and translational risk analysis.

In clinical development, AI supports patient stratification, trial feasibility, endpoint selection, dose optimization, and safety monitoring.

In postmarketing, AI supports real world data analytics, signal detection, subgroup analysis, and long term treatment performance.

In manufacturing, AI supports process monitoring, quality control, and production consistency.

The strategic opportunity is not to apply AI more broadly for its own sake. It is to apply AI where uncertainty is highest and decisions are most consequential, where better evidence earlier can improve validation, reduce development risk, and strengthen the basis for advancing the right therapies toward patients.

That is the standard by which AI in drug development will increasingly be measured.

title:
Let's make a concrete plan to 'cure every disease in 10y' and see how far we could get.

Our assumptions will be ~infinite IQ 200+ 'thinkers', automated labs by ~2032, $1-2T to spend (~10y Google prof
content:
Let's make a concrete plan to 'cure every disease in 10y' and see how far we could get.

Our assumptions will be ~infinite IQ 200+ 'thinkers', automated labs by ~2032, $1-2T to spend (~10y Google profits), can recruit any living person, significant influence over US Gov but not omnipotence.

There are three problems to solve:
1) Knowing how to cure a disease.
2) Making the medicine to do it.
3) Showing that you've done it (in humans).

Difficulty on this timeline is 3>1>>2. We will need to identify longest critical path timelines for each problem, and do things in parallel.

We'll use siRNA for loss of function and LNP mRNA for gain of function, because this gives access to every target in the genome and makes transition from knowing through drug design very fast (if you assume AI has enough training data zero shot a small molecule for any target, could use that as well).
We will need manufacturing capacity, which can be built while we sort out what to do, COVID-style. Number of disease x person cases to treat in US is ~1B, which would mean ~1000x current capacity, at cost of ~$100B and requiring ~5M workers. Let's assume the workers can be robots by our deadline date. Let's assume AI makes the molecules 20x more potent/gram, then this expansion could cover global demand.
Main limitation of these drug modalities is not reaching all cell types. To solve this we will have AI nominate conjugated ligands for all cell types based on existing scSeq + proteomic Atlases, create libraries of these and use pooled in vivo screening of a whole organism to thoroughly map biodistribution for each. We'll prototype in primates to get methodology down, then will confirm using 3-5 human decedents (has been done for AAV serotype screens).  5-100B dollars depending on how deep you go on cell count. These conjugates will ~modularly map to any oligo sequence we come up with later. From experience this could be done in <3y.

Showing effects in humans will be the slowest part, particularly for progressive and hard-to-measure disease like Alzheimer's. To make our timeline we will have to develop at minimum prognostic and pharmacodynamic biomarkers for every disease where readouts take >2y. Let's assume doing multiple -omics on blood contains patterns that AI can infer as disease activity. 
You might pair this with video records of people with/without disease (either as new study in parallel, or get CCTV from China maybe), assuming AI can track behavioral & functional capacity as added data.
We want access to samples with causal information on disease, ideally timecourse with incidence of lots of diseases. The US Veteran's Admin has blood samples over many years from many many veterans. We'll spend year 1 working with USG to produce multi-omic data to pair with these health records, as has been done at mid scale with UK Biobank. By year 3 this could give us potential prognostic markers for all diseases. We'll come back to these.

For question 1, any sound thinker will tell you that some interventions will treat some cells while messing up others. So we will need two sets of data: First, understand every treatment's effect in every cell. We (today, only @GordianBio) can do this with pooled in vivo screening, in animals that have already developed the diseases to avoid waiting, to understand what does good/bad things in each cell type. 
In parallel, we will start testing safety of the treatments in healthy human volunteers, doing dose escalation of ~40 people x 20k x up/down at 50K per patient (just blood draws) would be like 80B dollars, and within order of mag of how many patients are recruited for (all) trials today (if you think this is daunting, spend 1y doing in mice first). From this we will 1) get toxicity for each target, 2) draw blood and get pharmacodynamic markers for each target, 3) measure blood changes for AI to compare to the VA data, as well as to the cellular changes from the pooled screen, to deconstruct the physiological changes from cellular effects.

So year 4ish you have treatments in animals that benefit each disease/cell type, you put together the data on which interventions cause which types of toxicity systemically with what effects occur in each cell types to learn what cell types to avoid for each target, and use biodistribution data to design around that.
This tells you what interventions where, so you use and/or combine those into trials in diseased patients (~600B for 25K diseases, 4 treatments per), initially with multiple treatment arms for each of your hypotheses and biomarker readouts based on the blood omics for efficacy potential. Get more blood, calibrate, pick best options.  Say 3 rounds of 1y trials. All paperwork and analysis ~instant because AI.
We'll try combinations too based on the causal in vivo map, using AI to identify synergies based on effects and inferring regulatory/interactome networks and cell-cell interactions.
If you're good at this you now have a strong treatment for each disease, could imagine running a pivotal with just one or two hundred patients, say 20M and 2y, 500B if 25K diseases (in reality less because most of those 25K diseases are rare+genetic).

Key thing is that the manufacturing scaleup, the delivery enablement, the target discovery, and the biomarker development happen in parallel in the first ~3-4 years, leaving time for a few rounds of biomarker-based trials and then one pivotal per disease.

We'll fall short of 'all diseases', missing: Ones not present in VA data, ones with no natural model system (although we should try ex vivo human organs), a few where neither KD or overexpression solves. 
FDA approval may have to wait a few more years to wait for pivotal trial hard endpoints if biomarkers not considered validated surrogates yet.

And of course everything has to go right, etc. etc. 
But there's at least directions we can start today that make amazing outcomes happen in our lifetimes.

(h/t discussions with @SGRodriques)

Introducing Tenet, our first model post-trained for legal.

Tenet is a Kimi K3 base that we post-trained with @FireworksAI_HQ on a corpus of publicly available legal data, synthetic data, and human ex
content:
Introducing Tenet, our first model post-trained for legal.

Tenet is a Kimi K3 base that we post-trained with @FireworksAI_HQ on a corpus of publicly available legal data, synthetic data, and human expert data simulating long-horizon legal work.

Training increases Tenet's all-pass rate by 82% on LAB and 22% on LAB Contracts relative to the Kimi K3 base model. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on LAB Contracts and places second on LAB.

These gains generalize to other leading agentic benchmarks including @mercor's Apex Agents - Corporate Law, @crosbylegal's Redline Bench, and @scale_AI's Professional Reasoning Bench.

Tenet is also optimized for token efficiency, operating at less than a fourth the cost of leading foundation models.

We additionally post-trained three specialist models for Tenet to use as subagents:

1) M&A Diligence: post-trained with @baseten on our LAB Diligence environment in an RLM harness, this model is optimized for high-scale, long-horizon tasks.

2) Review Tables: trained with @appliedcompute on our Review Table environment, this model is state-of-the-art and cost-effective at high-volume document review and structured data extraction.

3) Firm Knowledge: trained with @EngramLab on our synthetic law firm environment, this model is optimized to learn and search over a firm's knowledge via memory and structured notes.

More details on model training, environment design, benchmarking, results, and more in the article by @gabepereyra below.

What's next for Harvey’s research?
- Scaling LAB to more jurisdictions, practice areas and workflows
- Scaling compute to bring new generalist models and capabilities to Harvey

More to come soon.

One worker, a 28-year-old man from Anhui Provin
content:
This is not AI. 
On June 27, 2009, a 13-story residential building under construction in Shanghai’s Lotus Riverside community completely toppled over. 

One worker, a 28-year-old man from Anhui Province, lost his life in the incident.

Investigation later revealed that the cause was a massive 10-meter-high soil pile dumped on the north side of the building, while a 4.6-meter-deep basement excavation was underway on the south side. The resulting lateral pressure exceeded the pile foundation’s capacity, causing the structure to tip over.

All designs and materials were found to comply with standards.

Authorities responded swiftly — soil was removed, the excavation backfilled, and developer funds frozen. Responsible parties were held accountable, and buyers received compensation. The project was later taken over by Vanke and rebuilt by Shanghai Construction Group.

The incident shocked the nation and sparked widespread debate about construction safety standards in China.

title: According to Taiwan-based media outlet DigiTimes, suppliers in Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and China are expanding production capacity for higher-margin, advanced copper-clad laminates (CCLs) in respo
content:
According to Taiwan-based media outlet DigiTimes, suppliers in Taiwan, Japan, South Korea, and China are expanding production capacity for higher-margin, advanced copper-clad laminates (CCLs) in response to supply shortages, but the capacity additions are running behind schedule.

Supply-chain sources cited by DigiTimes said Taiwan’s Elite Material Co. (EMC) and South Korea’s Doosan Corporation Electro-Materials BG have each seen their CCL equipment installation schedules delayed by about six months. Construction delays were cited as the cause at EMC, while Doosan’s delay followed a workplace safety incident at a construction site.

Taiwan Union Technology (TUC) has also experienced delays. Equipment delivery problems in the second quarter of 2026 pushed back mass production for the second phase of its Thailand plant by roughly two months. Nevertheless, production began in July, with shipments expected to increase from August as the plant ramps up.

These delays suggest that high-end CCL shortages and extended lead times are unlikely to ease in the near term.

Production capacity for AI server PCB-grade CCL remains concentrated among a small group of Tier 1 suppliers, including Taiwan’s EMC, TUC, and Nan Ya Plastics; Japan’s Panasonic Industry; South Korea’s Doosan; and China’s Shengyi Technology. With upstream material supplies also tight, lead times for high-end CCL have reportedly stretched to four to six months.

Supply-chain sources expect Doosan to be the sole supplier of CCL for compute boards during the initial production ramp of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin server platform. Meanwhile, Nan Ya is expected to join Shengyi and EMC in supplying materials for Vera Rubin switch boards.

There’s one thing I genuinely like about @KaitoAI and @axisrobotics:

They’re not simply chasing narratives — they’re trying to solve real bottlenecks.

For @KaitoAI, it’s not just about building another AI tool. Kaito is turning attention into measurable, usable data. Yaps looks beyond simple follower counts or impressions, focusing on relevance, engagement, and insight.

In a market where attention is becoming one of the most valuable assets, I think this is a very interesting direction.

And @axisrobotics is tackling a completely different, but equally important problem:

Physical AI needs DATA.

A robot can have powerful hardware, advanced models, and massive compute — but without diverse real-world data, it’s difficult for intelligence to truly evolve.

Axis is building an open data infrastructure that brings together simulation, human contributions, and model training to create a growing data flywheel.

One is helping quantify human attention.

The other is helping build machine intelligence.

What interests me most isn’t the hype today.

It’s the bigger question:

Can these infrastructures become part of the foundation for the next generation of the internet and AI?

Personally, I’ll keep watching both @KaitoAI and @axisrobotics.

Not simply because the narratives are hot.

But because I believe the projects solving real problems are the ones worth paying attention to.

title:
AlphaFolding: 4D Diffusion for Dynamic Protein Structure Prediction with Reference and Motion Guidance

1. AlphaFolding introduces a 4D (space + time) score-based diffusion model that predicts an enti
content:
AlphaFolding: 4D Diffusion for Dynamic Protein Structure Prediction with Reference and Motion Guidance

1. AlphaFolding introduces a 4D (space + time) score-based diffusion model that predicts an entire protein trajectory at once: up to 32 time steps simultaneously for proteins up to 256 residues, instead of generating frames iteratively.

2. The method is trained on molecular dynamics (MD) simulation trajectories and targets dynamic structure prediction rather than static folding or equilibrium conformation sampling, aiming to reproduce temporally ordered motions and conformational transitions.

3. A unified representation is used for full-atom dynamics: backbone motion is modeled with per-residue SE(3) frames, while side chains are reconstructed via rigid atom grouping and explicit prediction of 7 torsion (dihedral) angles per residue, enabling backbone + side-chain trajectories.

4. The diffusion process is defined on SE(3) across residues and time steps, with separate stochastic processes for rotations (SO(3)) and translations (R3), and a denoising score network trained with denoising score matching plus auxiliary geometric losses.

5. Reference guidance is implemented via a dedicated reference network: latent embeddings from an initial 3D reference structure are injected into the denoising network through a spatial module, improving structural consistency during motion generation.

6. Motion guidance is implemented via a motion alignment module: stacked temporal transformer self-attention aggregates information across adjacent frames (including preceding motion steps), improving temporal coherence and reducing abrupt transitions between predicted frames.

7. The architecture builds on protein-geometry ideas (e.g., invariant point attention) with iterative updates of node/edge features and frames; sequence conditioning uses GeoFormer-derived residue node/edge embeddings plus diffusion time embeddings.

8. Benchmarks include ATLAS (filtered to 758 structured proteins from 1,390) and a fast-folding set (Chignolin, Trp cage, BBA, Villin, BBL, protein B). Two evaluation regimes are used: short-term-to-long-term extrapolation (S2L) and generalization to unseen proteins (O2O).

9. Reported Cα-RMSE improvements over DFF and Flow-Matching baselines are strongest at long horizons. On ATLAS S2L, R32 error drops to 2.12 Å (vs 4.60 Å for FM). On fast-folding S2L, R32 is 4.39 Å (vs 5.48 Å for FM). Ablations show motion alignment reduces error (e.g., ATLAS R2 from 1.40 to 1.30 Å).

10. Simultaneous multi-step generation improves both accuracy and runtime scaling versus iterative rollouts: inference time stays roughly constant as trajectory length increases (reported ~7 seconds), while iterative methods accumulate error and cost with longer rollouts.

📜Paper: https://t.co/MzcVlH3h6C
